auditor.name: V. K. Beswal & Associates
qualifications_or_emphasis: The Company has not transferred Debenture Interest for FY 2006-07 amounting to Rs. 8,486/- to the Investor Education and Protection Fund as required under Section 124 & 125 of the Companies Act, 2013.

We have relied on the audited accounts for the Financial Year 31st March 2026 as provided to us by the Company. We have not verified the correctness and appropriateness of financial records and Books of Accounts of the company.

The Compliance of the provisions of Corporate and other applicable laws, rules, regulations, standards is the responsibility of management. Our examination was limited to the verification of procedure on test basis.

Emphasis of Matter – Ind AS 19: Employee Benefits - Company has not made provision for post-employment defined benefit obligations on actuarial basis as required under Ind AS 19. Management views impact as not material due to limited employees and modest benefit expenses. Opinion not modified.
key_audit_matters: Existence of Inventories and Trade Payable (in respect of Inventory): As at 31st March, 2026, the Company purchased finished cloth (traded goods – fabric) aggregating Rs. 8,42,83,550/- from its supplier, due to unforeseen commercial reasons, the sale of the said goods could not be executed during the financial year ended 31st March, 2026. Valuation, existence, and the propriety of the provision for purchase return identified as Key Audit Matter given: (a) significant judgement involved in determining the quantum of the provision (80%) and the assessment of Net Realisable Value (NRV) of the remaining 20% inventory; (b) goods are lying at the supplier's warehouse with no independent third-party physical verification possible; (c) material impact of the provision on Inventories, Trade Payables and Purchases.
Inventory lying at supplier's warehouse with 80% provision for expected returns and 20% carried at NRV
Non-provision for post-employment defined benefit obligations (Gratuity and Compensated Absences) as required under Ind AS 19

outlook.statement: The future for the textile Industry looks promising, buoyed by strong domestic consumption as well as export demand. Free trade with Asian countries and proposed agreements with EU Countries will also help to boost exports. Also, the west has started taken India seriously as a potential supplier of polyester yarn apart from China. Rising government focus and favourable policies to support the industry has led to growth in the industry.

risks: High cost of manufacturing and taxation
Fluctuations in foreign exchange adversely impacting exports and long-term export orders
Uncertainty in exchange rates making it difficult to purchase machinery from abroad
Adequate availability of raw material at right prices crucial; disruption in supply or violent changes in cost structure would affect profitability
Government's periodical announcements for liberalised tariff concessions offered to least developed countries like Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and other countries under SAFTA
Indian Textile Industry is highly fragmented
Competition in domestic and world markets especially from China
Lack of technological development affecting productivity
Cost competitiveness and low margins due to recessionary trends in developed countries
Technological obsolescence in weaving and spinning sector
Power shortage in some states affecting plant utilisation and causing volatility in yarn prices
Increasing input costs i.e. power, finance and logistics
